# Title: How are individuals with prediabetes managed in Denmark, and which patient characteristics are associated with receiving recommended management?

## Background

Prediabetes and type 2 diabetes (T2D) represent a growing public health challenge worldwide. In Denmark, nearly 19,000 individuals are diagnosed with T2D each year, contributing to more than 250,000 people living with the disease. In addition, approximately 60,000 individuals are estimated to have undiagnosed T2D, while nearly 300,000 people are living with prediabetes.

Prediabetes is an intermediate state of dysglycaemia associated with an increased risk of developing T2D and cardiovascular disease. Depending on the diagnostic criteria applied, approximately 10–40% of individuals with prediabetes progress to T2D within 1–5 years, whereas 17–45% revert to normoglycaemia without developing diabetes.

Large randomized clinical trials have demonstrated that intensive lifestyle interventions, including dietary modification, increased physical activity, and weight reduction, can substantially reduce the risk of progression from prediabetes to T2D. Despite this evidence, Denmark currently has no national clinical guidelines specifically addressing the management of prediabetes. Current practice is generally limited to recommendations for annual HbA1c monitoring, lifestyle modification, and referral to municipal preventive programs when considered appropriate. As a result, the management of prediabetes may vary considerably between healthcare providers and across healthcare sectors.

Despite the increasing prevalence of prediabetes, little is known about how individuals are managed in routine clinical practice in Denmark. In particular, it remains unclear whether individuals are informed about their diagnosis, offered structured follow-up, or referred to preventive interventions in accordance with current recommendations. Furthermore, patient characteristics associated with receiving recommended management remain largely unexplored.

Understanding current management practices is essential to identify potential gaps in care and inequalities in the delivery of preventive healthcare. Identifying patient groups who are less likely to receive recommended management may help inform future national recommendations and improve the implementation of preventive care for individuals with prediabetes.

Therefore, the primary aim of this study was to describe the current management of prediabetes in Denmark from the patient's perspective, including communication of the diagnosis, follow-up, referral to preventive interventions, and participation in preventive programs. The secondary aim was to examine the association between different management strategies and lifestyle behavior among individuals with prediabetes.

## Methods

### Data sources

Data were obtained as part of the DP-Next prospective cohort study. Participants underwent a standardized clinical examination including a questionnaire specifically developed for this study. The questionnaire collected patient-reported information on communication of the prediabetes diagnosis, follow-up, referral to preventive interventions, participation in interventions and lifestyle behavior following the diagnosis of prediabetes.

### Study design

This study is a cross-sectional study within the ongoing DP-Next prospective cohort study. Questionnaire data were collected at the time of the participants' clinical examination to assess the management of prediabetes, including communication of the diagnosis, follow-up, referral to preventive interventions, and self-reported lifestyle modifications.

### Study population

The study population consisted of adults aged 40–50 years participating in the ongoing DP-Next prospective cohort study. Individuals were eligible for inclusion if they had prediabetes, defined as a HbA1c level of 42–47 mmol/mol, and attended the DP-Next clinical examination. Participants who completed the study questionnaire were included in the present analysis. Participants with missing questionnaire data were excluded.

### Exposure

The primary exposures were patient-reported management strategies following a diagnosis of prediabetes. These included communication of the diagnosis, offer of follow-up, referral to preventive interventions, and participation in preventive programs.

Communication of the diagnosis was assessed according to whether participants had been informed of their diagnosis and the healthcare professional providing the information. Follow-up was assessed as whether participants had been offered repeat HbA1c testing or other structured follow-up after the diagnosis. Referral to preventive interventions was assessed as whether participants had been referred to municipal lifestyle programs or other preventive initiatives. Participation in preventive interventions was categorized as full participation, partial participation, or no participation.

### Outcome

The primary outcomes were patient-reported measures of prediabetes management, including communication of the diagnosis, offer of follow-up, referral to preventive interventions, and participation in preventive programs.

Secondary outcomes included patient-reported lifestyle behaviours assessed using the International Physical Activity Questionnaire Short Form, dietary habits, alcohol consumption and smoking status.

### Confounders

Potential confounders included age, sex, body mass index (BMI), HbA1c, educational level, socioeconomic status, health literacy and family history of type 2 diabetes. These variables were selected prior, based on their potential association with both prediabetes management and lifestyle behaviours.

### Statistical analysis

Baseline characteristics were summarized using means with standard deviations for continous variables and frequencies with percentages for categorical variables. The primary analyses will describe patient-reported management of prediabetes.

Secondary analyses will examine the association between patient-reported management strategies and lifestyle behaviours. Depending on the distribution and type of outcome, continuous outcomes will be analysed using linear regression and categorical outcomes using logistic regression. Multivariable models will be adjusted for predefined confounders.

A two-sided p-value \<0.05 will be considered statistically significant. Statistical analyses will be performed using R version XX (R Foundation for Statistical Computing, Vienna, Austria).
